notes:
Maintainer risk: HIGH — the workspace's 'caller identity' foundation seam is defined but multiple core handlers (Space/join, SpaceInvite/set, SpaceBan/set, CustomEmoji/set, Message/set reaction-modification) write or check account_id where the spec requires the caller's ChatContact.id (principal_id). Single-user mode hides the bug; first multi-user deployment will surface it as cross-user authorization failures and identity-leakage. Compounded by zero permission enforcement on SpaceInvite/set and SpaceBan/set (spec-mandated manage_members and ban gates entirely absent) and ChatContact/set update accepting non-whitelisted fields. The /set/get visibility surface for SpaceInvite and SpaceBan returns whole-account contents to any caller, violating spec scoping. Findings split between handler-side and reference-backend-side, with several rooted in trait shape (e.g. invite redemption can't be globally scoped without a new ChatBackend method). These are not 'polish' issues; they are spec-correctness gaps that the kit's own integration tests do not exercise because every test uses single-user MemoryBackend with no identity wired.
Confidence: ~70% chance of missed bug. Least confident flags: JMAP-x2gd.5 (reaction sender identity — depends on Reaction wire-type semantics I only partially verified) and JMAP-x2gd.16 (is_contact_blocked direction — depends on which side of a direct chat owns the ChatContact record, which the spec is slightly ambiguous on for federated peers). Uncertainty driven by: (1) the chat draft spec is large (1757 lines) and I sampled spec passages rather than full-reading; (2) I did not exercise the integration.rs test file at 6563 lines — there may be tests that already catch some of these in ways that contradict my reading; (3) the federation draft is separate and may shift identity semantics for cross-server users in ways relevant to several findings here; (4) I read the diff against fca0c74 holistically but did not commit-by-commit walk the 60-commit history, so I may have missed regressions vs older behavior that the workspace tested for once and then forgot. Would raise confidence if: (a) a manual spec-walk of every wire field's identity semantics (ChatContact.id, principal_id, accountId) was done with citations; (b) integration tests were rewritten to use an IdentityBackend with two distinct principals per account, surfacing every identity-confusion finding here at compile/test time; (c) the chat-federation draft was cross-checked for cross-server identity flow.
API contract risk: MEDIUM — the workspace's correctness, immutability, and consumer-facing-shape posture is mostly defended (ChatLimits / EmojiSetOp use #[non_exhaustive], generate_invite_code has CSPRNG mandate, permissions module is pure-helper-only, foundation re-exports are properly #[non_exhaustive] upstream). Notable gaps are concentrated on three smaller types (SlowModeError, OpResult, MemoryError) and on one type-system-vs-doc divergence (expire_message Ok-on-not-found via SHOULD-prose vs typed NotFound variant). The serde_json::Map leak in apply_space_metadata_patch and the ClosureHandler re-export are textbook leakage findings. The cap-enforcement split is the workspace-architectural finding most likely to be revisited as a fix rather than waved off.
API contract confidence: ~25% chance of missed issue. Least confident flags: JMAP-x2gd.36 (generate_invite_code — the length/charset/fallibility contract gap is real, but my recommended async-fallible rewrite may conflict with the trait's sync-method ergonomics; a senior reviewer might prefer documenting the length contract and keeping sync) and JMAP-x2gd.44 (cap-check split — the handler-side pre-flight is documented as 'MAY enforce caps a second time for defense in depth' so the workspace may push back as 'working as intended' rather than a contract gap; the engineering basis stands but the fix has policy implications). Uncertainty driven by: (1) I did NOT sample crate-jmap-mail-server's analogous trait shape to verify the canonical-template propagation lens; several findings (SlowModeError, OpResult, MemoryError, ClosureHandler re-export) likely have mail-server analogs that would re-classify them as workspace-wide convention bugs rather than chat-server-local findings; (2) I did NOT cross-check whether kith/stoa (the two named consumer crates) actually compile against jmap-chat-server today — if they have already worked around the contract gaps via Cargo.lock pinning or feature flag gymnastics, that mitigates the severity but doesn't change the contract risk for third parties; (3) I did NOT examine jmap-server's re-exports (SetError, BackendSetError, SetErrorType, etc.) for their own contract gaps — those are out-of-scope for this review (since the epic is scoped to chat-server) but their shape leaks into chat-server's public API and could be the root cause of contract pressure I attributed to chat-server. Would raise confidence if: (a) a cross-check of mail-server's backend.rs verified whether SlowModeError-shape and OpResult-shape patterns recur there with the same omissions (raising those to workspace-sweep priority), (b) a downstream-consumer compile of kith + stoa against this revision was attempted to surface any compile-time contract pressure the kit had hidden, (c) a 'simulated third-party' exercise wrote a non-trivial 50-line custom ChatBackend impl against just the public docs (no source-reading), to catch contract gaps that only surface from the outside-in perspective.
API contract supplement (2nd pass, 2026-05-13): 6 additional api-contract findings filed as .46-.51, none marked opinion. Pass focused on the public surface beyond backend.rs (which the 1st pass concentrated on): lib.rs re-exports, permissions module, helpers internals, and the 3121-line memory.rs reference backend. Key supplementary findings: (1) ChatBackend::supports_type signature lacks account_id while its doc explicitly promises per-account semantics — a strictly more severe form of the .43 'limits is sync' defect because here the production fix is not even available via override; (2) may_set_custom_emoji returns Result<bool,Error> with no path for deployment-specific rejection reason, a regression against the workspace's elsewhere-established rich-SetError pattern; (3) MemoryBackend::register_account leaks test scaffolding into the regular public surface without #[doc(hidden)] or production-banner, and 4 of 9 sibling _for_test methods have inconsistent stability signaling; (4) SlowModeError is named *Error but lacks std::error::Error + std::fmt::Display impls, breaking standard composition with ? / anyhow / thiserror / tracing %-formatter; (5) JMAP-x2gd.43's enumeration of which trait methods are sync was wrong — 4 more methods (supports_type, generate_invite_code, protect_last_admin, retains_edit_history) are also sync, expanding .43's complaint to a 5-method pattern. Overall verdict: same MEDIUM as the prior pass. The contract is not safe to call 1.0-stable yet but is structurally defensible. None of the supplement findings change the migration story for downstream consumers significantly; all are pre-1.0 movable.
API contract supplement confidence (2nd pass, 2026-05-13): ~20% chance of missed issue. Lower than the 1st pass's 25% because the 1st pass had already swept backend.rs (where most of the deep contract gaps live) and the 2nd pass focused on the smaller perimeters of lib.rs (~290 lines), permissions.rs (~140 non-test lines), and memory.rs (~430 lines of public-surface declarations, rest is impl). Least confident flags: (a) JMAP-x2gd.47 (may_set_custom_emoji bool→reason loss) — the recommended fix (nested Result or Option<SetError>) imposes ergonomic cost on backends doing the trivial case, so the workspace may push back as 'design intent: bool=cheap, escape hatch via Err for the rare case'; the engineering basis stands but it is the most aesthetic-adjacent of the six; (b) JMAP-x2gd.49 (test-helper signaling inconsistency) — this is documented as 'pattern is the documented intent, deviations are bugs', but a reviewer who weights consistency lower than I did could downgrade to opinion. Uncertainty driven by: (1) I did NOT cross-check whether jmap-mail-server (the canonical extension-server template, per the AGENTS.md banner that fired mid-task) has analogous sync hooks (supports_type, etc.) or a SlowModeError-equivalent without Error/Display — if it does, several of .46-.51 are workspace-wide convention bugs rather than chat-server-local, which would re-classify them up to higher priority and into a propagation epic; (2) I did NOT read every line of memory.rs (the explore subagent did the enumeration, I trusted the public-surface table without verifying every line); (3) I did NOT compile a 50-line custom ChatBackend against just the rustdoc to surface contract gaps that only appear from the outside-in perspective — the 1st pass's confidence note explicitly called this out as the highest-leverage missing exercise, and I did not perform it either. Would raise confidence if: (a) jmap-mail-server's BackEnd trait and ErrorBackendBootstrapTaskBuilder-shaped types were cross-walked for the same patterns (sync hooks, *Error without Error impl, register_account-shaped helpers); (b) cargo doc was actually rendered and read for the kit's public API, since #[doc(hidden)] vs not is most visible in cargo doc output; (c) the 50-line custom backend exercise from the 1st pass's confidence note was performed.
Rust idiom confidence (2nd rusty pass, 2026-05-14): ~25% chance of missed issue. Slightly lower than the 1st rusty pass's 30% because this pass:
(a) ran cargo clippy -p jmap-chat-server -- -W clippy::pedantic, which the 1st pass had explicitly called out as the highest-leverage missing exercise — that surfaced 236 warnings of which 7 distinct families merited findings;
(b) sampled memory.rs which the 1st pass entirely skipped — found the gratuitous-allocation pattern at Inner::current_state / objects_ref / objects_mut that the 1st pass flagged as the most likely miss site;
(c) cross-walked file sizes against jmap-mail-server (the canonical extension-server template) to verify which findings are chat-server-local vs. workspace-canonical — confirming that the big-handler pattern (.58) is workspace-canonical and shouldn't be fixed in isolation.

Least confident flags: JMAP-x2gd.52 (HashMap-key allocation pattern) — the recommended nested-HashMap fix imposes API change on Inner internals that might cascade through MemoryBackend's surface; a senior reviewer might prefer leaving the perf issue in the reference impl with a doc-comment 'production backends MUST restructure key layout' and treating it as deliberate teaching scaffolding rather than a defect. The engineering basis stands either way.

Uncertainty driven by:
(1) I did NOT verify whether jmap-mail-server's memory.rs (2742 lines, never sampled) has the same Inner-key-allocation pattern — if it does, .52 is a workspace-sweep, not chat-server-local; if not, chat-server has drifted from canonical. A 1-grep check would resolve this and I did not run it.
(2) I did NOT run cargo clippy --workspace -- -W clippy::pedantic (only -p jmap-chat-server). A workspace-wide pedantic run would surface whether .54 (manual_let_else) and .56 (rustdoc polish) are workspace-pervasive — if they are, those findings up-prioritize because the sweep is bigger but the per-bead cost stays the same.
(3) I did NOT sample integration.rs (4708 lines) or any tests/. Test-code idiom misses are lower-stakes (tests are not on the public API surface), but a serious Rust shop would flag .unwrap() vs .expect() with diagnostic text, helper-fn duplication, etc. The 1st pass's confidence note also flagged this gap and I did not close it.
(4) I did NOT compile a 50-line custom ChatBackend against just the rustdoc to surface contract-shaped findings (the highest-leverage exercise per BOTH the 1st pass's confidence note and the API-contract 1st/2nd-pass confidence notes). That exercise belongs to a downstream-fit review, not a Rust-idiom review, but the rusty perspective would benefit from it too.
(5) clippy::nursery and clippy::cargo were NOT run — they would surface a different class of findings (cargo metadata polish, nursery-grade idiom suggestions) that I have not investigated.

Would raise confidence if:
(a) jmap-mail-server's memory.rs was grep'd for the to_owned() / .clone() / Inner-key-allocation patterns, confirming or refuting the workspace-sweep classification of .52;
(b) clippy::pedantic was run workspace-wide so .54 and .56 could be filed against their canonical-propagation parents instead of chat-server alone;
(c) clippy::nursery and clippy::cargo were swept once for their distinct lint families.

- JMAP-x2gd.53 (P3): memory.rs query_objects i64/u64/usize as-casts
- JMAP-x2gd.54 (P3): manual_let_else x17 sweep

API contract risk (3rd pass, 2026-05-14): still MEDIUM — same posture as the 1st/2nd passes. 9 supplementary findings filed as .59-.67 covering the three high-leverage exercises the prior passes' confidence notes explicitly flagged as missing: (a) the mail-server canonical-template cross-walk (.67 re-classifies 7 prior findings .35/.38/.43/.46/.47/.48/.51 as workspace-canonical, not chat-server-local), (b) the 50-line custom-backend mental exercise (.59 surfaced 5 critical implementer-contract gaps in the most-used foundation methods create_object / update_object / destroy_object, which all prior passes overlooked because they audited from inside-out not outside-in), (c) the Cargo.toml/metadata audit (.61 absent docs.rs config, .63 realistic-demo-ids feature undocumented, .66 getrandom direct dep). Three further docs/underspecified findings (.60 bd:JMAP-* tracker IDs in published rustdoc, .62 protect_last_admin UpdateMember-strip case, .64/.65 apply_space_metadata_patch underspecification) round out the pass. None marked opinion — every finding has engineering basis that would survive a code-review thread. The contract is structurally defensible but the kit's docs-as-contract surface still has notable gaps in the consumer-perspective view; the foundation-methods doc thinness (.59) is the single highest-leverage doc change suggested by this exercise.
API contract supplement confidence (3rd pass, 2026-05-14): ~12% chance of missed issue. Lower than the 1st pass's 25% and the 2nd pass's 20% because this pass closed the three highest-leverage exercises the prior confidence notes explicitly flagged: mail-server cross-walk, consumer-perspective foundation-methods read, and Cargo.toml/metadata audit. Remaining uncertainty is bounded by:

Least confident flags:
(a) .64 (apply_space_metadata_patch Ok(None) semantics) and .65 (SetErrorType selection vagueness) — I did NOT cross-check whether mail-server's analogous method has the same ambiguities. If yes, both should be re-parented as workspace-canonical alongside .67's seven. A 1-grep check of mail-server's update_object docs would resolve this and I did not run it.
(b) .62 (protect_last_admin UpdateMember case) — engineering basis stands but the actual reference MemoryBackend impl may already extend the check to UpdateMember role-strip; if so the doc gap shrinks from 'spec-correctness gap' to 'doc-fidelity gap'. Did not verify.
(c) .66 (getrandom direct dep) — P4 and may be intentional (no other consumer exists today). A maintainer who weights workspace-deps-consistency lower than I did could downgrade to opinion.

Uncertainty driven by:
(1) I could NOT actually render cargo doc (the slash command's read-only rule forbids writes anywhere including target/doc/). The docs.rs gap (.61) and the intra-doc-link assertions are inferred from source, not from seeing the rendered HTML. A real downstream-fit review would render and inspect.
(2) The mail-server cross-walk surfaced six new patterns (N1-N6 in .67's body) that I marked as mail-server-LOCAL but did not grep chat-server for. Spot-check: chat-server's create_object does NOT appear to have N1's placeholder-sentinel-input contract, but I read the doc once not deeply. Could be wrong.
(3) The 50-line custom backend exercise was mental, not compiled. The explore subagent walked the trait method-by-method and reported what an implementer would have to guess; but it did not actually write 50 lines of Rust and try to compile against the kit. A real exercise would catch contract-shape friction the mental exercise missed.
(4) I did NOT compare chat-server's .64/.65 underspecification against mail-server's apply_space_patch / update_object analogs — if mail-server has the same ambiguities, .64/.65 are workspace-canonical not chat-server-local.
(5) I did NOT examine the integration.rs (4708 lines) or any tests/ for whether the kit's own test suite catches any of the contracts that .59 flags as underspecified. If a test fixture demonstrates the expected behavior, that's evidence the contract exists 'in the test code' rather than the rustdoc — fixable by lifting the test fixture's intent into the doc.

Would raise confidence to ~5-8% if:
(a) cargo doc was rendered (presumably by a non-read-only downstream-fit reviewer) and the HTML inspected for layout breaks and intra-doc-link resolution;
(b) chat-server was grepped for analogs of mail-server N1-N6 (placeholder-sentinel-input, MUST-override prose contracts, quietly-serial default impls, bool returns losing error context, macro triplication, positional config knobs);
(c) mail-server's update_object docs were cross-walked for the Ok(None)-vs-Some and SetErrorType ambiguities to re-classify .64/.65 as workspace-canonical if they propagate;
(d) an actual 50-line custom backend was compiled-against-the-kit (not mental-walked) by a non-read-only reviewer, catching contract-shape friction that surfaces only when the compiler is the oracle.

At this point the diminishing-returns curve is steep — a 4th api-contract pass would likely produce <5 findings, most opinion-flagged. The contract review is converging; further investment goes to fixing rather than finding.

API contract risk (4th pass, 2026-05-14): still MEDIUM — same posture as the 1st/2nd/3rd passes. 10 supplementary findings filed as .68-.77, including 2 P1s on substantive undocumented backend contracts. Pass focused on the two read-only-doable exercises the 3rd-pass confidence note flagged as still-missing (mail-server N1-N6 chat-server grep + mail-server update_object cross-walk for .64) plus a new exercise: tests-as-implicit-contract-documentation across the 7 integration test files (~10,800 lines total).

Key 4th-pass findings:
- .68 (P2): chat-server has 7 sites of `Id::from("placeholder")` sentinel usage in create_object handler paths; trait doc is silent. Worse than mail-server which explicitly documents the same pattern. This closes the JMAP-x2gd.67 N1 'spot-check could be wrong' uncertainty: chat-server DOES have N1, in 7 sites.
- .69 (P2): JMAP-x2gd.64 (update_object Ok(None)-vs-Some ambiguity) is workspace-canonical — the ambiguous doc sentence is BYTE-IDENTICAL in mail-server. Re-classify alongside .67's seven workspace-canonical findings.
- .70 (P2): apply_space_patch lacks per-op SetError variant table; tests at role_member_apply.rs:977-980 + :1003-1006 assert InvalidProperties for AddMember failures the doc characterizes as 'invalid id', a contract not in the published rustdoc.
- .71 (P2): apply_space_patch / apply_space_metadata_patch description content convention is encoded only in 4 tests, not in rustdoc. A backend that returns SetError::new(Forbidden) verbatim (as the doc literally suggests) fails the kit's own test suite.
- .72 (P1): RemoveChannel cascade to Message destruction + state bump entirely undocumented. Test at integration.rs:4102-4125 asserts it; rustdoc at backend.rs:441-509 is silent on cross-type cascade. Substantive correctness gap.
- .73 (P1): Category-cascade Chat/changes bump entirely undocumented. Test at integration.rs:3729-3733 asserts it. Comment at integration.rs:3677-3680 records this WAS a real bug fixed in bd:JMAP-g7wu.2.4.9; contract that prevents recurrence lives only in the test.
- .74-.77 (P3): four smaller doc tightenings on memberCount invariant, expire_message state non-bump, AddRole/AddCategory placeholder id, and the stale generate_invite_code default-impl reference at backend.rs:362-364.

The dominant pattern: chat-server's foundational write methods (apply_space_patch, apply_space_metadata_patch, create_object, update_object, expire_message) all carry tests that encode contracts the rustdoc does not. The doc-as-contract surface is materially thinner than the kit's actual behavior — by far the most common gap shape in this pass.

Recent commits since fca0c74 that addressed prior findings (#4cf642e, fdd83e7, c0f4a95, 85ca4fb, c64d655, 3164872, ac2f561, de2b2df, ee6b41e, ece17b3) were audited individually for new contract risks introduced by the fixes themselves; verdict: clean. Zero new P0/P1 findings from that audit. One borderline P2 observation (RequiredPermissions::Known carries &'static [&'static str], leaving permissions stringly-typed) was deemed consistent with workspace policy and not filed.

None of the 10 findings were marked opinion. .76 was the most borderline (the contract is partly implied by OpResult's 'new server-assigned id' wording) but the wire-shape with a writable id field makes the gap non-obvious and worth filing.

The single highest-leverage fix from this pass: one new 'Cross-type cascade contract' + 'Per-op error semantics' sub-section on apply_space_patch's rustdoc closes 5 of the 10 findings (.70, .71, .72, .73, .74). The remaining 5 are doc tightenings on smaller perimeters.
API contract supplement confidence (4th pass, 2026-05-14): ~8% chance of missed issue. Lower than the 3rd pass's 12% because this pass closed two of the three remaining read-only-doable exercises the 3rd-pass confidence note flagged as missing:

(b) chat-server grep for mail-server N1-N6 analogs: DONE — produced .68 (N1 match, worse than mail-server); N3/N4/N5/N6 confirmed no match; N2 partial-match on stale generate_invite_code rustdoc filed as .77.
(c) mail-server's update_object cross-walk for .64 / .65: DONE — .64 confirmed workspace-canonical (.69 filed), .65 confirmed chat-server-LOCAL (mail-server has no apply_*_metadata_patch analog because RFC 8621 has no permission-gated metadata sub-path on any object).
(d) actual 50-line custom backend compiled: NOT done (writes target/, forbidden by read-only rule). A careful tests-as-implicit-contract exercise on top of the 3rd-pass's .59 read closed most of what the compiled exercise would have surfaced, but not all — see uncertainty (3) below.
(a) cargo doc rendering: NOT done (writes target/doc/, forbidden by read-only rule).

Least confident flags:
(a) .76 (AddRole/AddCategory placeholder id) — engineering basis stands but a reviewer who weights 'partly implied by OpResult new server-assigned id wording' more heavily could downgrade to opinion. Held as P3 not opinion because the wire shape with a writable id field makes the gap non-obvious to a careful reader.
(b) .69 (update_object workspace-canonical reclassification) — the cross-walk was textual diff of two doc blocks; I did NOT cross-check whether the same byte-identical sentence recurs in jmap-calendars-server, jmap-tasks-server, jmap-contacts-server, etc. (the other 6 extension-server siblings have not been authored yet, so no risk on this front, but if/when they are authored from the mail-server template they will carry the same gap).
(c) .77 (generate_invite_code stale rustdoc) — small finding, factually correct but borderline-opinion. Held as P3 not opinion.

Uncertainty driven by:
(1) The mental cross-walks for tests-as-contract (.70-.77) were sampled on 7 test files, totaling ~10,800 lines. The exploration subagent reported finding 8 candidate gaps; one (.76) was borderline and was filed; the other 7 were filed as .70-.75/.77. Sample size is good but not exhaustive — there may be additional contract gaps in tests/common/ helpers, in tests/space_get_projection.rs (which the exploration explicitly reported as well-documented but did not exhaustively sweep), or in test fixtures that exercise rare boundary cases.
(2) The recent-commits audit checked 10 commits since fca0c74 against newly-introduced contract risks. I trusted the explore subagent's per-commit verdicts after spot-checking 2 of the 10 in detail. A more thorough pass would re-read each commit's diff individually; for an api-contract review the spot-check-plus-trust pattern is acceptable because the fixes were narrow.
(3) Compiled-against-the-kit exercise still NOT performed. A real third-party who writes a 50-line ChatBackend impl against just the rustdoc would surface contract gaps that a mental walk through the trait does not — specifically around what happens when the implementer has to choose between two equally-plausible API uses for a sub-feature. The mental walk catches obvious gaps; the compile catches subtle ones. This remains a gap on every api-contract pass and would need a non-read-only follow-up review to close.
(4) cargo doc rendering still NOT performed. The .61 docs.rs config gap and intra-doc-link assertions are inferred from source, not from seeing rendered HTML. A real downstream-fit review would render and inspect; this is also reserved for a non-read-only follow-up.
(5) I did NOT cross-check whether the 'tests-encode-contracts-that-rustdoc-does-not' pattern from .70-.77 recurs in mail-server. If mail-server's MailBackend trait + tests have the same per-op SetError variant gap, the same cascade gap, the same description content gap, etc., findings .70-.75 should be re-parented as workspace-canonical alongside .67 and .69. A 1-grep check against jmap-mail-server tests/ for assert!(desc.contains(...)) and assert_eq!(... destroyed) would resolve this; not done this pass. This is the single highest-priority unclosed exercise.

Would raise confidence to ~3-5% if:
(a) jmap-mail-server tests/ were grepped for the four key assertion patterns (cascade destruction, state bumps, per-op SetError variant, description substring match) to determine whether .70-.75 propagate to mail-server as workspace-canonical;

At this point the diminishing-returns curve is steep. A 5th api-contract pass would likely produce <3 findings, most opinion-flagged or workspace-canonical-propagation of patterns already filed. The contract review has converged; further investment goes to fixing (apply the doc tightenings in .68-.77, propagate .69 and the open question (5) above to mail-server) rather than finding.

Crypto-security supplement (1st pass, 2026-05-16): ~12% chance of missed P0 — a competent third-party crypto reviewer running the same checklist would, with low probability, find a P0 I did not flag. Justification for this number rather than higher:

The crate's actual crypto surface is structurally narrow. After mapping every secret-bearing type, every constant-time compare, every CSPRNG consumer, every untrusted-input boundary, every logging site, and every cryptographic primitive (sections A-G of the supplement), the crate's surface reduces to:

- one secret (`SpaceInvite.code`), one constant-time compare (subtle::ConstantTimeEq at space.rs:1325), one CSPRNG consumer (getrandom at memory.rs:826), zero hashes, zero MACs, zero signatures, zero AEADs, zero KDFs, zero ciphers
- zero `tracing::*` / `log::*` / `println!` / `eprintln!` / `dbg!` calls in the entire crate
- zero crate-defined Display impls that interpolate secret fields
- zero `.unwrap()` on attacker-supplied bytes in production paths
- no auth, no persistence, no transport — the kit is transport-less by intentional design (workspace AGENTS.md "What this workspace builds")

So the surface where a P0 could hide is bounded: the invite-code lifecycle (generate → store → wire-emit → store → ct_eq compare), the per-Space patch parser allocator (which I flagged at P2), the redaction-discipline gaps (which I flagged at P1), and the unchecked Id::from(s) pattern (P2).

Findings filed (7 total):
- .91 (P1): backend Display leak in chat.rs:336-340 + message.rs:853-864 missed by redaction sweep
- .92 (P2): Vec::with_capacity(arr.len()) memory-DoS amplification in parse_structural_entries
- .93 (P2): unchecked Id::from(s) bypasses RFC 8620 §1.2 validation workspace-wide
- .94 (P2): ChatBackend trait silent on invite-code storage discipline
- .95 (P3): inviteCode wire input not length-capped before clone
- .96 (P3): reference-backend SetError descriptions interpolate serde_json::Error
- .97 (P3): SpaceInvite.code lacks redacting Debug in jmap-chat-types (latent for downstream)

Sections spent < 10 min on:
- Section G (algorithm / parameter choice) — 5 min. The crate has only 2 crypto-adjacent primitives (CSPRNG via getrandom, ct_eq via subtle). Both were verified by the exploration subagent and need no additional inspection. Reading more deeply is unlikely to surface new findings.
- Section E (persistent storage) — 5 min. The kit is persistence-less; the reference MemoryBackend stores everything in-memory. Storage-side encryption is the consumer's concern per the AGENTS.md kit posture. The one contract-shaped concern (storage discipline of the invite code itself) is filed as .94.

Sections spent appropriate time on:
- Section A (key material lifecycle) — read every secret-bearing type's derives. Surfaced .97.
- Section B (side-channel hygiene) — verified the one ct_eq site and that no plain `==` exists on secrets. The length-discrimination side-channel is documented in code at space.rs:1317-1322; already-acknowledged trade-off, not a finding.
- Section C (untrusted-input boundaries) — exhaustive map produced by exploration subagent; surfaced .92 (Vec allocation), .93 (Id::from), .95 (inviteCode), and a handful of length-cap gaps that are workspace-canonical patterns mostly covered by sibling-crate handling and the kit's transport-less posture.
- Section D (random source quality) — verified the one CSPRNG site at memory.rs:826 (getrandom::fill, 16 bytes, documented panic-on-fail). The demo_next_id non-CSPRNG path is feature-gated and explicitly demo-only.
- Section F (logging output safety) — exhaustive grep produced zero log calls in src/. The risk surface is the redaction discipline for wire-bound error descriptions. Surfaced .91 (the main P1).

Sections where I read all relevant code paths vs. only the diff:
- Read all of `src/space.rs`, `src/chat.rs`, `src/message.rs`, `src/invite.rs`, `src/memory.rs` (invite-code paths), `src/helpers.rs` (redaction helpers), `src/backend.rs` (trait surface) — these are the crypto-surface bearing files.
- Cross-walked `crate-jmap-mail-server/src/mailbox.rs` (.91 canonical-divergence check) — confirmed mail-server uses server_fail_from_backend correctly at the analog site.
- Did NOT exhaustively read 6900+ lines of `tests/integration.rs`. Crypto defects in test code don't bear on production posture.
- Did NOT read `jmap-chat-types/src/space.rs` SpaceInvite definition directly — relied on the exploration subagent's report that Debug is derived. The finding .97 is therefore one inferential step removed; if Debug is actually a manual redacting impl in chat-types, .97 is invalid and should be closed.

Probability calibration: ~12% chance of missed P0.

Least confident flags:
- .94 (storage discipline) — the engineering basis stands, but a maintainer who weights "reference impl gets it right, production backends figure it out" higher than I did could downgrade to opinion. The actual fix is a doc tightening, low cost.
- .93 (unchecked Id::from) — the workspace-canonical fix is option (b) in the finding (move From<String>/From<&str> behind pub(crate) or rename to from_unchecked). That's a moderate API change that touches every handler in every extension-server. A reviewer might prefer option (a) per-handler change as too churn-heavy.

Uncertainty driven by:
(1) I did NOT verify `jmap-chat-types` source for the SpaceInvite Debug derive directly (.97). The finding is inferential.
(2) I did NOT cross-walk `crate-jmap-mail-server/src/memory.rs` SetError construction sites to confirm whether .96's pattern recurs there (would re-classify as workspace-canonical).
(3) I did NOT run a tracing / observability dependency-tree audit across jmap-chat-server's transitive deps. The crate has no direct tracing dep but the `subtle`, `getrandom`, or `serde_json` deps could conceivably pull tracing transitively; if so, a future-`tracing::*`-instrumentation regression test would benefit from a workspace-wide log-capture canary at the chat-server level. Did not file a finding because the kit has zero log calls today.
(4) I did NOT verify the chat-server tests/common harness (FaultyBackend, TrackingBackend, IdentityBackend) for whether the test scaffolding itself leaks invite codes through Debug or println. Per the exploration, no log calls exist in tests/, but the test code does use `format!("{:?}", invite)` patterns in assertion paths. Test-code leak is not a production exposure but could mask a regression.
(5) I did NOT compile-test against the rustdoc-only contract of `ChatBackend` from an outside-the-kit author's perspective (the same gap that prior API-contract passes left open). The crypto-security perspective on this would surface "what happens if a backend gets the storage discipline wrong" with compiler-style detail; the .94 finding is mental-walk derived.

Would raise confidence to ~5-8% if:
(a) `jmap-chat-types/src/space.rs` `SpaceInvite` Debug derive was directly verified (closing .97 inference);
(b) `crate-jmap-mail-server/src/memory.rs` SetError sites were cross-walked to determine if .96 propagates as workspace-canonical;
(c) the workspace-wide `subtle` and `getrandom` audit was extended to all sibling crates (no direct evidence of issues, but a workspace-canonical lens would close this gap);
(d) tests/common harness was audited for invite-code in Debug-format assertions;
(e) the workspace AGENTS.md "Security testing" §1 + §2 canary patterns were applied to `SpaceInvite` (which would surface .97 with engineering-test-grade certainty rather than inference).

At this point the diminishing-returns curve is steep — a 2nd crypto-security pass would likely produce 0-2 findings, most opinion-flagged or workspace-canonical-propagation. The crypto surface of this kit is small and the high-value patterns have been covered.
